lessons.title: Preparing for a germination test
lessons.html:
Preparing for a germination test

The germination test tells the farmer how many seeds in a lot can grow into normal plants under good conditions. It is the figure printed on the seed label that most farmers check first. A maize lot with low germination means gaps in the land and lost yield, so the test must be done carefully and the same way every time.

The work area

  • Clean and disinfect benches, counting boards and trays according to laboratory procedure, so that fungi from a previous test do not spread.
  • Check that germinators or germination rooms are at the temperature and light conditions set in the testing rules (usually ISTA rules) for the crop, and that the temperature records are up to date.
  • Check the water supply. Use water of the quality your procedure requires.
  • Have the right substrate ready: paper towels, blotters, sand or a mix, depending on the crop and method.

The planting sample

Germination is tested on seeds taken from the pure seed fraction of the purity analysis, or from the sample as the procedure says. The rules set how many seeds to plant, often in replicates, for example several replicates of a set number of seeds each.

  1. Mix the pure seed well.
  2. Count out the replicates at random, by hand or with a counting board or vacuum counter. Do not pick only the best-looking seeds.
  3. Label each replicate with the sample number, replicate number and planting date.

Documentation

Open a germination worksheet for the sample. Record the crop, cultivar, lot and sample number, the method (for example between paper, top of paper or sand), the temperature, any pre-treatment such as pre-chilling for dormant seed, the planting date and the dates for the first and final counts. These dates come from the testing rules for that crop.

Planning workload

A busy seed laboratory may start hundreds of tests a week before the planting season. Plan germinator space, label everything and never stack trays in a way that blocks air flow or light.

lessons.title: Planting and caring for the test
lessons.html:
Planting and caring for the test

How the seeds are planted has a big effect on the result. Too much water causes rot; too little stops germination. Seeds too close together let fungi spread from seed to seed.

Common methods

MethodTypical use
Top of paperSmall seeds, for example many vegetables and grasses
Between paper (rolled towels)Larger seeds such as maize, sorghum, beans
Sand or soilSeeds that are hard to evaluate on paper, or to confirm a result

The testing rules state which methods are allowed for each crop.

Planting steps

  1. Wet the substrate evenly to the moisture level in your procedure. Pour off extra water.
  2. Place seeds evenly spaced, not touching, in the layout set for the method.
  3. For rolled towels, cover the seeds with a second towel, roll loosely and stand the rolls upright in a labelled container or bag.
  4. Place replicates in the germinator at the correct temperature and light conditions.
  5. Record the time the test went in.

Care during the test

  • Check moisture regularly. Add water if the substrate is drying out, but do not flood it.
  • Check germinator temperature records daily.
  • Look for spreading fungi. Mouldy seeds that are clearly dead may be removed and recorded at counts to stop them infecting others, as your procedure allows.
  • If dormancy is suspected, follow the rules for treatments such as pre-chilling or other approved methods.

Safety

Some seed is treated with fungicide or insecticide, often coloured red, green or blue. Wear gloves when handling treated seed, do not eat or drink at the bench and wash hands after work. Follow the treatment label for handling precautions.

lessons.title: Evaluating seedlings and completing the test
lessons.html:
Evaluating seedlings and completing the test

At the first and final count dates you evaluate each seedling. The question is not only whether the seed sprouted, but whether it produced a seedling that could grow into a healthy plant in the field.

Categories

  • Normal seedlings: all essential structures present and healthy, such as a good root system, shoot and the leaves or cotyledons typical of the crop.
  • Abnormal seedlings: damaged, deformed or decayed, for example no main root, a split or twisted shoot, or a seedling rotted by a primary infection.
  • Hard seeds: seeds that stayed hard because they did not take up water, common in legumes such as lucerne and clover.
  • Fresh ungerminated seeds: seeds that took up water and stayed firm but did not germinate, often dormant.
  • Dead seeds: soft, mouldy or decayed seeds that produced nothing.

Use the seedling evaluation handbook your laboratory follows. When unsure, ask a senior analyst.

Counting

  1. At the first count, remove and record normal seedlings that are clearly well developed.
  2. Leave doubtful seedlings for the final count.
  3. At the final count, evaluate everything remaining in every category.
  4. Record the results for each replicate separately.

Calculating the result

Calculate the average percentage of normal seedlings across the replicates. Check that the replicates agree within the tolerance in the testing rules. If they do not, the test must be repeated. Report the percentages of normal seedlings, abnormal seedlings, hard, fresh and dead seeds as required.

Completing the process

  • Complete and sign the worksheet and pass it on for checking.
  • Dispose of used substrate and seedlings as your procedure says, especially if seed was treated.
  • Clean and disinfect trays and the germinator space.

Key points

  • Clean, disinfected equipment and correct germinator conditions are the base of a reliable test.
  • Count replicates at random; never select the best seeds.
  • Keep the substrate moist but not flooded and check temperature daily.
  • Only normal seedlings count towards germination percentage.
  • Replicates must agree within tolerance or the test is repeated.
